title: Open Science in the Swedish Context
text:
Course syllabus


 Description The 1hp course ‘Open Science in the Swedish Context’ is designed to teach DDLS research school scientists how to apply Swedish Open Science standards in their daily research. The course covers key stages of the research lifecycle, from planning a research project, to sharing results, to science communication and researcher evaluation. Through interactive lectures, guest speakers, and practical assignments, participants will explore pre-registration, Open Access publishing, up-and-coming researcher evaluation criteria, and citizen science. Completing this training will prepare DDLS students to lead the global shift toward open and collaborative research.


 Prerequisites To follow this course, learners should have basic knowledge of: 1. Principles of scientific research and methodology 2. How research outputs are typically disseminated, (e.g., journals, conferences etc.) 3. The structure of the Swedish research system, including universities and funding bodies


 Learning Outcomes 1. Get acquainted with Open Science principles and how they will be implemented into Swedish academia within the coming years 2. Develop a foundational understanding of how to apply Open Science principles at key stages of a research project

 Target Audience: Researchers in the SciLifeLab DDLS program


 Level: Beginner


 License: CC BY 4.0

title: Assignment 1: The Swedish academic framework
text:
About



Purpose:
Familiarise participants with the Swedish legal and institutional context in which Open Science operates.
Learning outcomes:
Upon completion of this assignment, participants will be able to:

Identify the main institutions that govern Swedish research and higher education.
Describe the roles and responsibilities of researchers, universities, and funders in the Swedish system.
Explain the implications of Lärarundantaget (teacher’s exemption) on academic work. Understand the principle of public access to official documents (Allmän handling) and how it affects research.

Estimated duration:
120min

title: Assignment 1: The Swedish academic framework
text:
The Swedish academic system
Before diving into Open Science, it helps to understand how research in Sweden actually works. Laws, funding models, and institutional responsibilities shape what you as a researcher can and cannot do, often in ways that are not immediately visible in your everyday work. Knowing the basics of the Swedish research system makes it easier to understand your rights and responsibilities as a researcher, and provides important context for later discussions about sharing data, publications, and other Open Science practices.

Who sets the rules?
At the national level, the Government and the Riksdag (the Swedish parliament) are responsible for higher education. They:






Set the legal framework for universities and university colleges, mainly through two laws:

The Higher Education Act, which sets out the mission of higher education, academic freedom, and institutional responsibilities
The Higher Education Ordinance, which provides more detailed rules on degrees, admissions, employment, and study programmes.

The Government also sets the strategic direction for Swedish research through a national research policy bill, published every four years. The current bill (2025–2028) outlines priorities such as research excellence, internationalisation, and innovation, and shapes how public research funding is distributed.









Allocate public funding to universities, with education and research funded separately.
Research & PhD education funding comes from:

Recurrent government funding (base grants to universities)
External competitive funding, awarded by public agencies and other private research funders and organisations.
Almost half of all external funding comes from the Swedish government through research councils, in particular:

the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet)
the Swedish Research Council for Health, Working Life and Welfare (Forte)
the Swedish Research Council for Sustainable Development (Formas)
Sweden’s Innovation Agency (Vinnova)
the Swedish Energy Agency (Energimyndigheten)











Supervise higher education and research providers to ensure compliance with national legislation
Several (independent) government agencies under the Ministry of Education and Research are responsible for supervising universities and research activities in Sweden:

The Swedish Higher Education Authority (Universitetskanslersämbetet, UKÄ)supervises higher education institutions to ensure they comply with applicable legislation, including the Higher Education Act, the Higher Education Ordinance, the Administrative Procedures Act, and their own internal regulations.

The Swedish Council for Higher Education (Universitets- och högskolerådet, UHR) works with admissions, recognition of qualifications, international mobility, and information about higher education, rather than supervision of research quality.
The Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten)
Evaluates research involving humans, biological material, or sensitive personal data. Researchers must submit study plans for ethical review and approval before such research can begin.





🎓 PhD takeaway: Your PhD is shaped by national laws, not just local practice. Funding structures influence how research is organised and public-sector rules apply to most universities.



What is the role of universities?
Universities and university colleges have a broad mission that includes:

Education based on research or artistic practice
Research and development work
Interaction with society, so that research and knowledge benefit the wider community

In addition, Swedish higher education institutions have to guarantee researchers academic freedom. This means that researchers and teachers should be free to choose research questions, methods, and how results are communicated, within the legal framework.
Although Sweden’s higher education system is nationally regulated, universities are given a lot of freedom in how research and education are carried out. The Government sets overarching goals, but institutions decide independently how to meet them. For early-career researchers, this means that day-to-day research life is shaped largely by your university and your role within it. Universities independently decide:

How they are organised
Which courses and programmes to offer
The content and design of education
How many students to admit
What research to prioritise

There is thus no nationally fixed curriculum and no central planning of how much research or education should be done in specific fields. For PhD students, this also means that conditions can vary between universities. though three academic positions – professor, senior lecturer, and associate senior lecturer – are regulated by law. Under the Higher Education Act, researchers are free to choose research problems, develop methods, and publish results. The Act also emphasises academic credibility and good re search practice, along with the responsibility of higher education institutions to safeguard and promote academic freedom.

title: Assignment 1: The Swedish academic framework
text:
## Important actors
Part 2: Key Research Institutions and Funding Bodies Estimated time: 15–20 minutes
Swedish National Data Service (SND) Data repository for research data; supports data management Researchers deposit and access data
Universities Implement policies, supervise researchers, manage grants Day-to-day administration of academic work Reflection: Consider which of these institutions you interact with the most and why. Part 3: Roles and Responsibilities Estimated time: 10–15 minutes Understanding who is responsible for what is key: Researchers: Uphold academic freedom and research integrity Comply with legal obligations and funder requirements Manage and report data and publications responsibly Universities: Support researchers with policy guidance and infrastructure Supervise PhD students and staff Ensure compliance with national laws and funder requirements Funders: Define grant conditions and priorities Monitor compliance and reporting Provide guidance on best practices Tip: These roles are interlinked. A failure in one often impacts the others. Part 4: Legal Principles Affecting Academic Work Estimated time: 15–20 minutes 1. Lärarundantaget (Teacher’s Exemption) Swedish law allows teachers to freely use and publish materials they create for teaching. Implications: Teaching materials may be exempt from certain sharing obligations, but this does not override ethical or legal requirements for research data. 2. Allmän handling (Public Document) Many documents held by public authorities (including universities) are considered public. Principle of Public Access: Anyone may request access to official documents. Implications: Research records, communications, and reports may be accessible unless legally restricted (e.g., privacy, sensitive data). Tip: Researchers must balance transparency with confidentiality obligations. Part 5: Key Policy and Guidance Documents Estimated time: 10–15 minutes Some of the most important national documents include: The Higher Education Act (Högskolelagen) – governs universities, academic freedom, and responsibilities. Swedish Research Council guidelines – includes research ethics, open access recommendations, and data management. Freedom of the Press Act / Principle of Public Access – foundation for public access to documents. National guidelines for research integrity – defines good scientific practice. Exercise: Skim the Swedish Research Council website and identify one guideline relevant to your research area: https://www.vr.se Part 6: Assignments / Knowledge Checks Estimated time: 30–40 minutes 1. Actor Map Create a table or simple diagram showing: Key institutions (from Part 2) Their roles Who they interact with (researchers, universities, funders) 2. Scenario Questions You created slides for a university lecture. A colleague wants to post them online. Which legal principle may apply? Your research group receives a public request for internal communications. How should you respond? 3. Document Scavenger Exercise Go to https://www.vr.se or https://snd.gu.se. Find: One document that explains university responsibilities in research One guidance document about handling public requests 4. Reflection (Optional) “How do Swedish legal and institutional frameworks shape your day-to-day work as a researcher or student?”
Sources: https://www.uka.se/swedish-higher-education-authority/about-higher-education/governance-of-higher-education

Open Access publishing is the widely adopted ideal that all should have equitable access to the information generated by research.
There are six different types of OA publishing currently recognized. Below is an overview of the different types.
